nameStory: This delicate spurge earned the name 'graceful' from its elegant, flowing growth habit and the way its slender branches seem to dance in the breeze. The species name 'hypericifolia' means 'leaves like Hypericum' (St. John's wort), referring to the similar oval leaf shape. It's also called golden spurge for the yellowish tinge that sometimes appears on its foliage.
description: Graceful spurge is a low-growing perennial herb that spreads into loose, airy mats up to 2 feet tall. This tropical American native has found its way to New England, though it's still quite uncommon here. Like all spurges, it contains a milky white sap that can irritate skin and eyes, so it's best admired from a respectful distance. The plant has a delicate, almost wispy appearance with small oval leaves and tiny flowers.

idTips.label: Milky Sap
idTips.description: Break a stem and you'll see thick, white, latex-like sap ooze out - this is the telltale spurge family signature, but don't touch it as it can cause skin irritation

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged alternately along the stems, often with a slight yellowish or golden tint, smooth to the touch and about thumbnail-sized

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, spreading mats with slender, branching stems that have a graceful, almost flowing appearance as they bend and curve

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers clustered in small groups - they're actually specialized flower structures called cyathia that lack true petals

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish-tinged stems that feel somewhat succulent and bend easily without breaking

habitat: In New England, graceful spurge is found in disturbed soils, garden edges, and waste places where the ground has been turned over. It prefers sandy or well-drained soils and often appears in areas with some human disturbance. Being a warm-climate native, it's quite rare in our region and most likely to appear in protected, sunny spots.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the base, with fresh green stems and leaves appearing as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full foliage and tiny flowers blooming throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: May show yellowish coloration before frost kills back the above-ground portions of the plant.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, surviving as underground parts in milder areas, though often doesn't survive New England winters.

funFact: The milky sap that makes spurges irritating to touch was actually used by ancient fishermen as a fish poison - they would crush spurge plants upstream, and the sap would temporarily stun fish downstream, making them easy to catch by hand!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with spotted spurge, but graceful spurge has a more upright, flowing growth habit while spotted spurge stays flat on the ground. Memory trick: graceful spurge lives up to its name by growing gracefully upward, while spotted spurge spots the ground by hugging it closely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spurge,' these plants are completely unrelated to the seaweed called sea spurge or any other plants with 'spurge' in the name outside the Euphorbia family. The irritating sap has led to spurges being both valued as medicinal plants and feared as skin irritants throughout history.
compareHints: Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat. Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the rounded leaves with red spots of spotted spurge, graceful spurge has unmarked oval leaves. Its flowing, branched growth habit is more elegant than the rigid stems of flowering spurge.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
